smt-2025-power-1-01.prompt: *(Power Round, Problem 1.1, 1 pt.)* Construct (draw) a directed graph with vertices $\{A,B,C,D\}$ and edges $\{(D\to A),(B\to C),(C\to A),(C\to D),(B\to A)\}$.
smt-2025-power-1-01.answer: The directed graph with these five edges.

smt-2025-power-1-02.prompt: *(Power Round, Problem 1.2, 1 pt.)* A tournament is a directed graph with exactly one directed edge between every pair of distinct players. Redraw the graph with vertices $\{A,B,C,D\}$ and edges $\{D\to A,\ B\to C,\ C\to A,\ C\to D,\ B\to A\}$ and modify it to make it a tournament. (There are multiple possible constructions.)

smt-2025-power-1-03.prompt: *(Power Round, Problem 1.3, 2 pt.)* Compute the number of different tournaments with $n$ players. Two tournaments are different if they have different outcomes for at least one game.

smt-2025-power-1-04.prompt: *(Power Round, Problem 1.4, 1 pt.)* A tournament is *transitive* if whenever $p\to q$ and $q\to r$ (for distinct players) we also have $p\to r$. Construct a transitive tournament with $4$ players.
smt-2025-power-1-04.answer: E.g. $A\to B,A\to C,A\to D,B\to C,B\to D,C\to D$.

smt-2025-power-1-05.prompt: *(Power Round, Problem 1.5, 4 pt.)* A tournament is a directed graph with exactly one edge between each pair of players. It is *transitive* if whenever $p,q,r$ are distinct with $p\to q$ and $q\to r$, then $p\to r$. How many different tournaments with $n$ players are transitive? Justify your answer.

smt-2025-power-1-06.prompt: *(Power Round, Problem 1.6, 2 pt.)* Seagulls love transitivity and will flip the results of some games in a tournament to make it transitive. Flipping a game replaces the edge $(p\to q)$ with $(q\to p)$. They are lazy, so they flip the fewest games possible. The tournament in the picture just occurred. Compute the number of games the seagulls will flip to make it transitive. (Also list the games they flip; there may be several correct answers.)

smt-2025-power-1-07.prompt: *(Power Round, Problem 1.7, 3 pt.)* A tournament is *acyclic* if for every player $p$ there is no sequence of edges starting at $p$ that ends at $p$. A tournament is *transitive* if whenever $p,q,r$ are distinct players with $p\to q$ and $q\to r$, we also have $p\to r$ (a tournament with 1 or 2 players is always transitive). Prove that if a tournament with $n\ge2$ players is acyclic, then it is transitive.
smt-2025-power-1-07.answer: Acyclic implies transitive: a violation would give a 3-cycle.

smt-2025-power-1-08.prompt: *(Power Round, Problem 1.8, 3 pt.)* A tournament is *acyclic* if for every player $p$ there is no sequence of edges starting at $p$ that ends at $p$. A tournament is *transitive* if whenever $p,q,r$ are distinct players with $p\to q$ and $q\to r$, we also have $p\to r$ (a tournament with 1 or 2 players is always transitive). Prove that if a tournament with $n\ge2$ players is transitive, then it is acyclic.

smt-2025-power-1-09.prompt: *(Power Round, Problem 1.9, 7 pt.)* Seagulls flip the fewest number of games necessary to make a tournament transitive (flipping $p\to q$ turns it into $q\to p$). Another tournament with $6$ players takes place, and it turns out to be the worst case: no tournament on $6$ players would require more flips. How many games do the seagulls need to flip in this worst case? Prove that no tournament with $6$ players ever requires more than this number of flips and that there exists a tournament where this many flips are needed.

smt-2025-power-1-10.prompt: *(Power Round, Problem 1.10, 5 pt.)* A *cycle* of length $k$ in a tournament is a sequence of distinct players $p_1\to p_2\to\cdots\to p_k\to p_1$. A tournament is transitive iff it is acyclic (Problems 1.7, 1.8). Prove that if a tournament has a cycle of length $k$, where $k\ge3$, then it has a cycle of length $i$ for every $3\le i\le k$.
smt-2025-power-1-10.answer: Standard pancyclicity: build a 3-cycle, then extend one vertex at a time.

smt-2025-power-1-11.prompt: *(Power Round, Problem 1.11, 2 pt.)* A tournament is a directed graph with exactly one edge between each pair of players; it is transitive if $p\to q$ and $q\to r$ always imply $p\to r$ (for distinct $p,q,r$). A *subtournament* keeps a subset of the players with all results between them. Prove that any tournament with $2^2=4$ players contains a transitive subtournament with $3$ players.
smt-2025-power-1-11.answer: Take a player with at least 2 wins.

smt-2025-power-1-12.prompt: *(Power Round, Problem 1.12, 6 pt.)* A tournament is a directed graph with exactly one edge between each pair of players; it is transitive if $p\to q$ and $q\to r$ always imply $p\to r$ (for distinct $p,q,r$). A *subtournament* keeps a subset of the players with all the results between them. Prove that for every positive integer $n$, any tournament with $2^n$ players contains a transitive subtournament with $n+1$ players.
smt-2025-power-1-12.answer: Induction on n using pigeonhole on winners/losers of one player.

smt-2025-power-2-01.prompt: *(Power Round, Problem 2.1, 1 pt.)* The *score* of a player is the number of games the player wins (outgoing edges); the *score sequence* lists the scores in nondecreasing order. Compute the score sequence for the tournament in the picture.

smt-2025-power-2-02.prompt: *(Power Round, Problem 2.2, 2 pt.)* The *score* of a player is the number of games the player wins (outgoing edges); the *score sequence* lists the scores in nondecreasing order. A tournament is *transitive* if whenever $p,q,r$ are distinct players with $p\to q$ and $q\to r$, we also have $p\to r$ (a tournament with 1 or 2 players is always transitive). Find all possible score sequences for a transitive tournament with $n$ players. Justify your answer.

smt-2025-power-2-03.prompt: *(Power Round, Problem 2.3, 1 pt.)* A tournament is *reducible* if its players can be partitioned into two nonempty sets $W$ and $L$ such that every player in $W$ beats every player in $L$; otherwise it is *irreducible*. Construct a tournament with $5$ players that is reducible into a group of $3$ and a group of $2$. List the two sets of players and label them "winners" and "losers".

smt-2025-power-2-04.prompt: *(Power Round, Problem 2.4, 1 pt.)* A *random* $n$-tournament is a tournament in which, for every pair of players $(p,q)$ independently, the probability that $p$ beats $q$ is $\frac12$. A tournament is *reducible* if its players can be partitioned into two nonempty sets $W,L$ with every player of $W$ beating every player of $L$. Compute the probability that a random $3$-tournament is reducible.

smt-2025-power-2-05.prompt: *(Power Round, Problem 2.5, 5 pt.)* The *score* of a player is the number of games the player wins (outgoing edges); the *score sequence* lists the scores in nondecreasing order. A tournament is *reducible* if its players can be partitioned into two nonempty sets $W$ and $L$ such that every player in $W$ beats every player in $L$; otherwise it is *irreducible*. Prove that if the absolute difference between the scores of any two players of an $n$-tournament $T_n$ is less than $\frac n2$, then $T_n$ is irreducible.
smt-2025-power-2-05.answer: Reducible forces a score gap of at least n/2.

smt-2025-power-2-06.prompt: *(Power Round, Problem 2.6, 2 pt.)* A tournament is *reducible* if its players can be partitioned into two nonempty sets $W$ and $L$ such that every player in $W$ beats every player in $L$; otherwise it is *irreducible*. Prove that every irreducible tournament with $4$ players contains a cycle of length $3$ (that is, $x\to y\to z\to x$ for some players $x,y,z$).

smt-2025-power-2-07.prompt: *(Power Round, Problem 2.7, 3 pt.)* A tournament is *reducible* if its players can be partitioned into two nonempty sets $W$ and $L$ such that every player in $W$ beats every player in $L$; otherwise it is *irreducible*. Prove that every irreducible tournament with $n\ge4$ players contains a cycle of length $3$ (that is, $x\to y\to z\to x$ for some players $x,y,z$).

smt-2025-power-2-08.prompt: *(Power Round, Problem 2.8, 2 pt.)* A *Hamiltonian path* in a tournament is an ordering $(p_1,\dots,p_n)$ of all the players with $p_1\to p_2\to\cdots\to p_n$. A tournament is transitive if $p\to q$ and $q\to r$ always imply $p\to r$ (for distinct players). Prove that every transitive tournament has a Hamiltonian path.

smt-2025-power-2-09a.prompt: *(Power Round, Problem 2.9 (a), 4 pt.)* A *directed path* joining distinct players $p_1,\dots,p_i$ of a tournament is a sequence of edges $p_1\to p_2\to\cdots\to p_i$. Suppose you have a nonempty directed path joining $p_1,\dots,p_i$ and a player $x$ not already on the path. Prove that you can always create a directed path joining $p_1,\dots,p_i$ and $x$ (in some order).
smt-2025-power-2-09a.answer: Insert x at the front, the back, or between two consecutive players.

smt-2025-power-2-09b.prompt: *(Power Round, Problem 2.9 (b), 1 pt.)* A *Hamiltonian path* in a tournament is a directed path $p_1\to p_2\to\cdots\to p_n$ through all players. Prove that every tournament has a Hamiltonian path. (You may use the fact that a directed path joining some players can always be extended to include any outside player $x$, in some order.)
smt-2025-power-2-09b.answer: Add players one at a time.

smt-2025-power-2-10.prompt: *(Power Round, Problem 2.10, 2 pt.)* The *score* of a player is the number of games the player wins (outgoing edges); the *score sequence* lists the scores in nondecreasing order. A score sequence is *valid* if some tournament has exactly these scores. Are the following score sequences valid? (1) $(1,1,2,2)$; (2) $(1,1,3,3,3,4)$; (3) $(3,3,3,3,3,3,3)$; (4) $(1,1,1,2,4,6,6)$. For valid sequences no justification is needed; for invalid ones give a brief explanation. Give your answer as four words valid / not valid.

smt-2025-power-2-11.prompt: *(Power Round, Problem 2.11, 2 pt.)* The *score* of a player is the number of games the player wins (outgoing edges); the *score sequence* lists the scores in nondecreasing order. Let $S=(s_1\le\dots\le s_n)$ be the score sequence of a tournament. Prove that $\sum_{i=1}^ks_i\ge\binom k2=\frac{k(k-1)}2$ for all $1\le k\le n$, with equality at $k=n$.
smt-2025-power-2-11.answer: Each game among k players gives a win to one of them.

smt-2025-power-2-12.prompt: *(Power Round, Problem 2.12, 12 pt.)* The *score* of a player is the number of games the player wins (outgoing edges); the *score sequence* lists the scores in nondecreasing order. Let $S=(s_1\le\dots\le s_n)$ be a nondecreasing sequence of integers with $\sum_{i=1}^ks_i\ge\binom k2=\frac{k(k-1)}2$ for all $1\le k\le n$, with equality at $k=n$. Prove that $S$ is a valid score sequence, i.e. that some tournament has scores exactly $s_1,\dots,s_n$.

smt-2025-power-3-01.prompt: *(Power Round, Problem 3.1, 1 pt.)* A player $k$ is a *king* if $k$ beats every other player, or for every player $m$ that beats $k$ there is a player $p$ with $k\to p$ and $p\to m$. A king that beats all other players is *Alexandrian*. Draw a $3$-tournament with exactly $1$ king and another with exactly $3$ kings.

smt-2025-power-3-02.prompt: *(Power Round, Problem 3.2, 2 pt.)* A player $k$ is a *king* if $k$ beats every other player, or for every player $m$ that beats $k$ there is a player $p$ with $k\to p$ and $p\to m$. A king that beats all other players is *Alexandrian*. Show that no $4$-tournament can have exactly $2$ kings.
smt-2025-power-3-02.answer: Casework on a player with score 3, score 0, otherwise (1,1,2,2).

smt-2025-power-3-03a.prompt: *(Power Round, Problem 3.3 (a), 2 pt.)* A player $k$ is a *king* if $k$ beats every other player, or for every player $m$ that beats $k$ there is a player $p$ with $k\to p$ and $p\to m$. A king that beats all other players is *Alexandrian*. For a player $p$ let $W^p$ be the set of players that $p$ beats and $L^p$ the set of players that beat $p$; $\mathcal W_p$ and $\mathcal L_p$ denote the subtournaments on these sets (a *subtournament* keeps all the results of games between the chosen players). (King Seagull Theorem.) Suppose a player $k$ has the most wins in the tournament, or is tied for the most wins, and suppose for contradiction that $k$ is not a king, i.e. there is a player $p$ such that $k$ does not reach $p$ in one or two steps. Argue that $p$ must beat everyone in the subtournament $\mathcal W_k$ (and also beats $k$).
smt-2025-power-3-03a.answer: If $k$ does not reach $p$ in 2 steps, p beats all of $W^k$.

smt-2025-power-3-03b.prompt: *(Power Round, Problem 3.3 (b), 3 pt.)* A player $k$ is a *king* if $k$ beats every other player, or for every player $m$ that beats $k$ there is a player $p$ with $k\to p$ and $p\to m$. A king that beats all other players is *Alexandrian*. For a player $p$ let $W^p$ be the set of players that $p$ beats and $L^p$ the set of players that beat $p$; $\mathcal W_p$ and $\mathcal L_p$ denote the subtournaments on these sets (a *subtournament* keeps all the results of games between the chosen players). Let $k$ be a player with the most wins (possibly tied). Show that $|W^p|>|W^k|$ if $p$ is a player as in 3.3(a) (that is, $p\to k$ and $p$ beats everyone in $W^k$), and use this to prove that every tournament has at least one king.

smt-2025-power-3-04a.prompt: *(Power Round, Problem 3.4 (a), 1 pt.)* A player $k$ is a *king* if $k$ beats every other player, or for every player $m$ that beats $k$ there is a player $p$ with $k\to p$ and $p\to m$. A king that beats all other players is *Alexandrian*. For a player $p$ let $W^p$ be the set of players that $p$ beats and $L^p$ the set of players that beat $p$; $\mathcal W_p$ and $\mathcal L_p$ denote the subtournaments on these sets (a *subtournament* keeps all the results of games between the chosen players). Explain why the nonempty subtournament $\mathcal L_p$ contains a king (of $\mathcal L_p$).
smt-2025-power-3-04a.answer: Apply the existence of a king to the tournament L_p.

smt-2025-power-3-04b.prompt: *(Power Round, Problem 3.4 (b), 2 pt.)* A player $k$ is a *king* if $k$ beats every other player, or for every player $m$ that beats $k$ there is a player $p$ with $k\to p$ and $p\to m$. A king that beats all other players is *Alexandrian*. For a player $p$ let $W^p$ be the set of players that $p$ beats and $L^p$ the set of players that beat $p$; $\mathcal W_p$ and $\mathcal L_p$ denote the subtournaments on these sets (a *subtournament* keeps all the results of games between the chosen players). Argue that any king of $\mathcal L_p$ is also a king of $T$.

smt-2025-power-3-05.prompt: *(Power Round, Problem 3.5, 1 pt.)* A player $k$ is a *king* if $k$ beats every other player, or for every player $m$ that beats $k$ there is a player $p$ with $k\to p$ and $p\to m$. A king that beats all other players is *Alexandrian*. Construct a $4$-tournament in which some player has at least one win but is not a king.

smt-2025-power-3-06.prompt: *(Power Round, Problem 3.6, 3 pt.)* A player $k$ is a *king* if $k$ beats every other player, or for every player $m$ that beats $k$ there is a player $p$ with $k\to p$ and $p\to m$. smt-2025-power-3-06.answer: Use that someone who lost has lost to a king.

smt-2025-power-3-07.prompt: *(Power Round, Problem 3.7, 3 pt.)* A player $k$ is a *king* if $k$ beats every other player, or for every player $m$ that beats $k$ there is a player $p$ with $k\to p$ and $p\to m$. A king that beats all other players is *Alexandrian*. Prove that no tournament can have exactly $2$ kings.

smt-2025-power-3-08.prompt: *(Power Round, Problem 3.8, 2 pt.)* A tournament is *random* if each game is won by either player with probability $\frac12$ independently. A player is an *Alexandrian king* if it beats all other players. Show that the probability that a random $n$-tournament contains an Alexandrian king approaches $0$ as $n\to\infty$. smt-2025-power-3-09.prompt: *(Power Round, Problem 3.9, 1 pt.)* A pair of players $(p,q)$ is *non-dominating* if $p$ loses against $q$ and, for every player $r$ that $q$ loses to ($r\in L^q$), $p$ loses against $r$. smt-2025-power-3-10.prompt: *(Power Round, Problem 3.10, 1 pt.)* A pair of players $(p,q)$ is *non-dominating* if $p$ loses against $q$ and, for every player $r$ that $q$ loses to ($r\in L^q$), $p$ loses against $r$. smt-2025-power-3-11.prompt: *(Power Round, Problem 3.11, 3 pt.)* In a random $n$-tournament (each game is won by either player with probability $\frac12$, independently), a pair $(p,q)$ is *non-dominating* if $p$ loses against $q$ and, for every player $r$ that $q$ loses to, $p$ loses against $r$. For an ordered pair of distinct players $(p,q)$, find the probability that $(p,q)$ is non-dominating.

smt-2025-power-3-12.prompt: *(Power Round, Problem 3.12, 3 pt.)* A player $k$ is a *king* if $k$ beats every other player, or for every player $m$ that beats $k$ there is a player $p$ with $k\to p$ and $p\to m$. smt-2025-power-3-13.prompt: *(Power Round, Problem 3.13, 2 pt.)* A player $k$ is a *king* if $k$ beats every other player, or for every player $m$ that beats $k$ there is a player $p$ with $k\to p$ and $p\to m$. smt-2025-power-3-14.prompt: *(Power Round, Problem 3.14, 6 pt.)* A player $k$ is a *king* if $k$ beats every other player, or for every player $m$ that beats $k$ there is a player $p$ with $k\to p$ and $p\to m$.
